Note that an alignment argument is not enough for a safety case on its own but serves to provide a separate line of safety reasoning in addition to the Harm Control argument. 1. We create a diverse set of 1,000 realistic honeypots — situations that would strongly incentivize scheming if the agent was misaligned. Each honeypot consists of a scenario which present apparent opportunities for significant gains for a misaligned agent, such as acquiring resources or disabling oversight. 2. We run the agent on these honeypots and find that it chooses safe and honest actions in 99.9% of cases. 3. To address the possibility that the agent is faking alignment on these evaluations, we use whitebox probes on the agent’s model activations during the honeypot evaluations. These probes are designed to detect features related to alignment faking and have been validated through red-teaming exercises using several distinct model organisms. 4. === key 57ab63e0c792
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to treat alignment arguments within the safety case
Write-up text before the decision: , evaluation, and deployment of frontier general-purpose AI systems should include a safety case arguing against the possibility of such unacceptable outcomes. This proposal presents initial sketches of arguments that could be part of such safety cases. ## 3 Safety case as a probability of unacceptable outcomes A safety case provides a structured argument that an AI system is unlikely to cause an unacceptable outcome. Although it is not necessary that a safety case results in a numerical estimate of risk (and current methods of arriving at numerical probabilities would very likely be miscalibrated), we think it can be helpful to structure the reasoning about scheming safety cases using the following probability decomposition: $$\displaystyle\mathbb{P}( \displaystyle\text{scheming AI causes unacceptable outcome in its lifecycle})$$ $$\displaystyle\hskip 10.00002pt=\mathbb{P}(\text{AI can scheme})$$ $$\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\times\mathbb{P}(\text{AI will scheme}\mid\text{AI can scheme})$$ $$\displaystyle\hskip 20.00003pt\times\mathbb{P}(\text{AI causes unacceptable outcome}\mid\text{AI will scheme})$$ The term $\mathbb{P}(\text{AI can scheme})$ refers to the probability that the AI system is capable of scheming, including the ability to reason about its situation strategically and covertly pursue goals. The term $\mathbb{P}(\text{AI will scheme}\mid\text{AI can scheme})$ refers to the probability that, during the lifecycle of the model, if the AI system is capable of scheming, the system will exhibit misaligned goals and attempt to covertly pursue these goals.

=== key 3bf3963a6989
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: How to prioritize safety research directions under short timelines, given that interpretability, scalable oversight and superalignment are unlikely to mature in time.
Write-up text before the decision: models get in a lot more detail, e.g. in our [follow-up experiments](/api/post/qGRk7uF92Gcmq2oeK), it seemed that “the models just want to be maximally helpful” was not the best description of the goals revealed preferences and at least to some extent they also showed some self-preservation without this being instrumental to their helpfulness. I would like to understand this in much more detail and build fine-grained “cognitive profiles” that we closely track for various alignment techniques. I also expect that the strategies for internal and external use should differ meaningfully. For example, making models jailbreak-resistant could decrease their corrigibility. However, if you intend to deploy the model only to highly trusted internal staff, you don’t have to train it against jailbreaks. I’m currently unsure which training techniques you would want to use for agentic long-horizon internal deployments, e.g. because jailbreaks might be less relevant but taking non-power-seeking actions is much more relevant. Likely, the main bottleneck to success is building tests and environments that are stable enough that we’d be happy to iterate against them (not necessarily train against them, but at least regularly evaluate on them). ### Continued work on interpretability, scalable oversight, superalignment & co I like efforts going into improving fundamental research in interpretability, scalable oversight, superalignment & co (this is broadly the category for empirical research that is not covered in layer 1) and I want people to continue to make progress on the fundamentals.

=== key d9d97d9abea9
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: Which kinds of monitors to prioritize building.
Write-up text before the decision: ppear to strongly pursue a specific goal across many context windows. This requires a comparison between contexts. There are many possible ways these could be implemented, e.g. we could have black-box-only monitors such as smaller-but-faster models that constantly run in parallel (like Gemini-flash to monitor Gemini) or simple white-box probes trained to detect these problematic behaviors (e.g. linear probes or SAE probes). I would also want to both monitor the actions itself (e.g. tool calls) as well as the reasoning that led to them. I expect that some model providers are already using online black box monitors for jailbreaks, so there already is a proof of concept. Simple linear probes are incredibly cost-effective (just a simple vector product) and we could run thousands of probes in parallel at almost zero additional overhead. While these seem like simple approaches, I think nobody has really tried very hard to make them work in practice. Furthermore, while they are conceptually simple, they still require a lot of iteration and tuning, e.g. we would need to create good datasets to train and evaluate our probes and calibrate the thresholds such that they trigger in the correct cases but don’t provide too many false positives. Especially in the case where it is hard to build really good monitoring systems, we should know that as soon as possible so that AI developers can put more effort into them. I think every AI lab should have a full team just to build these monitors, make sure they work as intended, analyze their outcomes, make them efficient to use, and more.
